My doctoral research brings together two complementary aims: predictive models seek an accurate structural estimate from a sequence, while generative models seek a distribution of plausible structures that represents diversity and uncertainty.

## Generating RNA Structural Ensembles

::: {.research-line}
**The question.**

How can a model produce multiple plausible RNA secondary structures conditioned on a nucleotide sequence rather than returning only one estimate?

**What I do.**

I develop conditional discrete diffusion models with two-dimensional neural architectures for sampling RNA secondary structures. My work includes reproducible training and sampling pipelines and ensemble-level evaluation using consensus, energy, and structural-diversity criteria.
:::

## Evaluating Generalization in RNA Prediction

::: {.research-line}
**The question.**

How should RNA structure predictors be evaluated when training and test sequences share different degrees of similarity or belong to different RNA families?

**What I do.**

I study family-aware and sequence-similarity evaluation regimes across RNA datasets. My contribution focuses on reproducible comparison of classical and deep-learning predictors and on identifying when apparent predictive performance depends on the composition of the evaluation split.
:::

## Biomolecular Ensembles Beyond RNA

::: {.research-line}
Through the **IDPfun2 Marie Skłodowska-Curie Staff Exchanges** collaboration, I also explore generative modeling of ordered and intrinsically disordered protein ensembles. This work connects computational sampling with energy-landscape interpretations grounded in statistical physics.
:::
